parts:
Hi, 

I have a 2-factor model. The first factor has 2 items and the second factor has 3 items. The factors are orthogonal to each other.

All loadings were significant and the model fit is great. So I wanted to evaluate measurement invariance based on 3 categorical groups. 

I followed the measurement insurance steps by constraining factor loadings then y-intercepts using the lavaan built-in arguments (i.e. group.equal). However, the second item in the first factor now has a p-value that is not significant. I'm not sure why. The standardised factor loadings look fine to me, and I expected the p-values to be significant.

Please can someone explain why would this happen? I tested out on the HolzingerSwineFord dataset and could not replicate the problem.

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: p-value of factor loadings in a measuring invariance analysis
parts: The first factor has 2 items and the second factor has 3 items. The factors are orthogonal to each other.

Then how is your model identified?  With only 2 indicators (and the factor is not substantially correlated with another factor), identification requires fixing both loadings to 1 (to estimate the factor variance), or at least to equality (if factor variance is fixed to 1).  You cannot test invariance in this case because in the configural model, all loadings are already equal (if fixed to 1), or at least statistically equivalent to being equal (i.e., you would not gain any df if you constrained loadings across groups because you would have to also free factor variances across groups).

I suspect the model is not identified, even if lavaan was unable to find evidence enough to issue such a warning.

http://ww.w.statpower.net/Steiger%20Biblio/Steiger02.PDF

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

On Wednesday, October 6, 2021 at 2:01:12 PM UTC+1 Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
The first factor has 2 items and the second factor has 3 items. The factors are orthogonal to each other.

Then how is your model identified?  With only 2 indicators (and the factor is not substantially correlated with another factor), identification requires fixing both loadings to 1 (to estimate the factor variance), or at least to equality (if factor variance is fixed to 1).  You cannot test invariance in this case because in the configural model, all loadings are already equal (if fixed to 1), or at least statistically equivalent to being equal (i.e., you would not gain any df if you constrained loadings across groups because you would have to also free factor variances across groups).

I suspect the model is not identified, even if lavaan was unable to find evidence enough to issue such a warning.

Positive df is a necessary, not sufficient, condition for identification.  The paper I linked to explains why this is not identified.  To identify it, you can fix f1 =~ 1*Q28_DISEASE_ID and run the models again to test invariance of the f2 measurements.

Or you could free the factor covariance, but I'm not sure why you are treating them as orthogonal.  Are the 2 f1 indicators truly uncorrelated with the 3 indicators of f2?  Even if the factor covariance is small, your sample size should be large enough that the model could be empirically identified by the between-factor indicator correlations.

Wow, that is indeed nearly zero.  Even with your large sample, I wonder whether empirical underidentification will persist if you free the covariance.  Another empirical check for a stable result is to use the current parameter estimates as starting values to estimate the parameters again.  If they change, then your model is not identified.  If they are identical, that is necessary but still not sufficient evidence that the model is identified.
